group.title: More idioms
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: A lot of anger or worry about something that is really very small.
examples: The row over the parking spaces was just {a tempest in a teapot}.
wrong: The war that destroyed three cities was only a tempest in a teapot.

words.meaning: Everything possible, with nothing left out.
examples: They had a band, fireworks, a huge cake: {the whole nine yards}.
wrong: The party was the whole nine yards: just a few chips and no music.

words.meaning: To get pulled deeper and deeper into a topic, losing track of time.
examples: I looked up one fact and {went down a rabbit hole} for three hours.
wrong: He went down a rabbit hole and lost interest in the topic after a minute.

words.meaning: A person who surprises everyone by being better than expected.
examples: The quiet new player turned out to be {a dark horse} and won the cup.
wrong: Everyone knew he would win; he was a real dark horse.

words.meaning: The real test that shows whether something works or is true.
examples: The {acid test} of the new road will be rush hour.
wrong: The acid test proved nothing, because it was the least important check.

words.meaning: The biggest part of something.
examples: The eldest son got {the lion’s share} of the money.
wrong: He got the lion’s share, so he had less than anyone else.

words.meaning: A long search that is hopeless because the thing cannot be found.
examples: The fake map sent us on {a wild goose chase} across the island.
wrong: It was a wild goose chase: we found the shop on our first try.

words.meaning: A belief or custom that people think must never be questioned.
examples: In this firm, the annual bonus is {a sacred cow}.
wrong: The rule is a sacred cow, so everyone criticizes it freely.

words.meaning: A person who acts in wild, unpredictable ways that can cause trouble.
examples: The new adviser is {a loose cannon} who says whatever he likes.
wrong: She is a loose cannon, always careful and completely predictable.

words.meaning: A person who spoils other people’s fun.
examples: Don’t be {a wet blanket}; come dancing with us.
wrong: He was a wet blanket, keeping everyone laughing and dancing all night.

words.lemma: put the cart before the horse
words.meaning: To do things in the wrong order.
examples: Buying furniture before finding a flat is {putting the cart before the horse}.
wrong: She put the cart before the horse by doing each step in the correct order.

words.meaning: To stop trying because you are happy with past success.
examples: After one hit album, the band {rested on their laurels} and never improved.
wrong: He rested on his laurels by training harder than ever after his win.

words.meaning: To annoy or upset someone, often by accident.
examples: His blunt email {ruffled a few feathers} in the office.
wrong: Her kind words ruffled his feathers and made him feel calm and happy.

words.meaning: To start something that causes many new problems.
examples: Asking about the old contract {opened a can of worms}.
wrong: The question opened a can of worms, so everything became simple and quiet.

words.meaning: A sudden success that does not last.
examples: Critics said the young singer was just {a flash in the pan}.
wrong: The shop was a flash in the pan; it has been busy for fifty years.

words.lemma: like a bull in a china shop
words.meaning: In a clumsy, careless way where care is needed.
examples: He went into the delicate talks {like a bull in a china shop}.
wrong: She handled the fragile vase like a bull in a china shop, with perfect care.
words.ipa: /laɪk ə bʊl ɪn ə ˈtʃaɪnə ʃɑp/

words.meaning: Said without any preparation.
examples: His best jokes were completely {off the cuff}.
wrong: She spoke off the cuff, reading every word from her carefully prepared notes.

words.meaning: A difficult subject that people argue about and try to avoid.
examples: Tax reform is {a hot potato} that no party wants to touch.
wrong: The weather was a hot potato that nobody ever disagreed about.

words.meaning: Directly from the person who knows best.
examples: I heard it {straight from the horse’s mouth}: the boss is leaving.
wrong: I got it straight from the horse’s mouth, from a stranger who had only heard a rumor.

words.meaning: Clear signs that something bad is going to happen.
examples: When sales fell again, he saw {the writing on the wall} and found a new job.
wrong: The writing on the wall showed the company had never been safer.

words.meaning: To enjoy a chance to do something freely, often criticizing.
examples: The press {had a field day} with the minister’s mistake.
wrong: Reporters had a field day, so they ignored the story completely.

words.meaning: To raise a false alarm so often that people stop believing you.
examples: If you {cry wolf} too often, nobody will come when you really need help.
wrong: He cried wolf by warning people only when there was real danger.

words.meaning: In trouble because someone is annoyed with you.
examples: He forgot their anniversary and is {in the doghouse} now.
wrong: She is in the doghouse because everyone is so pleased with her.

words.lemma: kick the can down the road
words.meaning: To delay dealing with a problem until later.
examples: The council keeps {kicking the can down the road} on the bridge repairs.
wrong: They kicked the can down the road by fixing the problem that very day.

words.meaning: To end a quarrel and become friends again.
examples: After years of silence, the brothers {buried the hatchet}.
wrong: They buried the hatchet and kept fighting for another ten years.

words.meaning: To have a private reason, often a grudge, for what you do or say.
examples: Ignore his review; he {has an ax to grind} with the author.
wrong: He has an ax to grind, so his opinion is completely neutral.

words.meaning: Something that costs a lot to keep but is of little use.
examples: The huge stadium became {a white elephant} after the games.
wrong: The white elephant was cheap to run and used every day.

words.meaning: To keep arguing about something that is already decided or finished.
examples: The plan was rejected, so stop {beating a dead horse}.
wrong: She beat a dead horse by raising a brand-new question nobody had discussed.

words.meaning: A guess made with almost no information.
examples: My answer was {a shot in the dark}, but it was right.
wrong: It was a shot in the dark because I had checked every fact twice.

words.meaning: To do something risky that is almost against the rules.
examples: The firm {sailed close to the wind} with its tax returns.
wrong: He sailed close to the wind by following every rule very carefully.

words.meaning: To blame or betray someone to protect yourself.
examples: When the plan failed, he {threw his assistant under the bus}.
wrong: She threw her team under the bus by praising them and taking the blame herself.

words.meaning: To act in a way that makes going back impossible.
examples: Don’t insult your boss when you leave; never {burn your bridges}.
wrong: He burned his bridges, so he can easily go back to his old job.

words.meaning: A shameful secret from the past.
examples: Every old family has {a skeleton in the closet}.
wrong: His skeleton in the closet was a prize he loved to tell everyone about.

words.lemma: put your foot in your mouth
words.meaning: To say something embarrassing or tactless by accident.
examples: I {put my foot in my mouth} by asking about her ex-husband.
wrong: He put his foot in his mouth with a perfectly polite and tactful remark.

words.meaning: To take a risk by saying or doing something others won’t.
examples: She {stuck her neck out} to defend the new employee.
wrong: He stuck his neck out by staying silent and safe.

words.meaning: To be slow to do something because you don’t want to.
examples: The landlord is {dragging his feet} over the repairs.
wrong: She dragged her feet and finished the job a week early.

words.meaning: Looking foolish because something went wrong.
examples: The experts who predicted a win were left with {egg on their faces}.
wrong: He had egg on his face because his prediction was exactly right.

words.meaning: To have a complaint you want to discuss with someone.
examples: I {have a bone to pick} with you about the bill.
wrong: I have a bone to pick with you, as I am completely happy with what you did.

words.meaning: A completely different matter from the one just mentioned.
examples: Riding a bike is easy, but racing one is {a different kettle of fish}.
wrong: The two jobs are a different kettle of fish because they are exactly the same.

words.meaning: To get rid of anger or energy by doing something active.
examples: After work he goes running to {blow off steam}.
wrong: She blew off steam by sitting still and saying nothing all evening.
